title: 'Abasa: look at your food
hook: let the human look at his food: rain, grain, grapes, olives, palms (80:24–32)
tomorrow: 'Abasa: the day a man flees his brother

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'Abasa, he frowned, and the blind man who came eagerly. Your line was turn to the one who came. Who did you turn toward? Day two hundred fourteen.
screen: `'ABASA — TURN TO THE ONE WHO CAME.`

segments.voice: Think about your last meal. Where did it come from? The honest answer for most of us is: a store, a delivery bag, a drive-through window. Maybe a plastic tray with a sticker on it. The food shows up already finished, with the whole story cut off. Somewhere there was rain, and dirt, and a seed, and months of sun, and people bent over in a field. None of that is on the sticker. 'Abasa, after the story of the frown, turns to a very different subject, and asks us to do something almost nobody does anymore. Today: look at your food.
screen: `A TRAY WITH A STICKER.` → `THE STORY CUT OFF.` → `LOOK AT YOUR FOOD.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-four, in Pickthall's words: Let man consider his food. Look at it. Then the surah tells its story backward, from the plate to the sky. We pour water down in showers. Then We split the earth open, in clefts. Then We cause grain to grow in it, and grapes, and green fodder, and olive trees and date palms, and gardens thick with trees, and fruit, and grasses. Provision for you, and for your animals. Rain, cracked soil, a sprout, a harvest. It reads like a slow-motion film of a seed. And it lands on two words: for you, and for your cattle. The whole cycle is described as a gift, set down in front of you. One word in that list is famous for a different reason. The word for grasses, abb. A well-known report says that 'Umar, one of the closest companions, read this verse and admitted he didn't know exactly what abb meant, and then decided not to force a meaning onto it. Scholars today mostly say it means pasture, the plants that animals graze. But the honesty is worth keeping: even the first generation said, sometimes, we don't know exactly. Notice where this passage sits. Right after the surah reminds the human being he was made from a drop, and asks why he is ungrateful. The answer to ingratitude isn't a lecture. It's: look at your plate. Just look. Trace one bite back to the rain. That's also why many Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after. Two small words to bracket the story.
screen: `LET MAN CONSIDER HIS FOOD.` · `RAIN, CRACKED EARTH, GRAIN, FRUIT.` · `ABB — EVEN 'UMAR WASN'T SURE.` · `BISMILLAH BEFORE, ALHAMDULILLAH AFTER.` · then, large: `LOOK AT YOUR FOOD.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, choose one thing you ate today, or will eat soon. A piece of bread, an apple, rice. Trace it backward: the kitchen, the store, the truck, the field, the hands that picked it, the sun, the rain, the seed. Go as far back as you can. When you reach the rain, stop, and just hold it. The bell holds the time.
'Abasa. He frowned, Surah eighty, which also says: let the human look at his food, rain to grain to fruit. Today's word.
Your line: look at your food. At your next meal, before the first bite, look at it for five seconds and think of the rain. Day two hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, eat with the right hand, and try not to waste food; these verses of 'Abasa are often recalled as a reminder that every meal begins with rain.

match.prompt: the story of your food, backward — tap the pairs.

myth: every word in 'Abasa was perfectly clear to the first Muslims
a well-known report says 'Umar admitted he didn't know exactly what abb meant.
the passage traces food back to rain
water poured down, earth split open, then grain, grapes, olives and palms.
the surah says the provision is for people only
it says for you and for your cattle.

fork.setup: 'Umar reads the word abb and isn't sure what it means. what does he do, according to the report?
options: admits he doesn't know and doesn't force one
fork.reveal: he admits it and lets it be. honesty about not knowing is part of how the first generation read.

original.note: Arabic: "his food," from ta'am, food, what is tasted (Qur'an 80:24).

trapdoor: what you thought: be grateful for food.
what it means: look at your plate and trace it back, rain, earth, seed, harvest; the whole cycle is a gift for you and your animals.

what a scholar hears: the report of 'Umar and abb is found in several tafsir works and in al-Hakim; qadb, green fodder, is another rare word in the list; the passage answers the ingratitude named in 80:17.
